name: keras
title: Keras: A Multi-Backend Deep Learning Framework for AI
answer: Keras is an open source Python deep learning framework maintained by the Keras team, released under the Apache 2.0 licence and described on its site as deep learning for humans. It sits at the model building layer of the AI stack, offering high level APIs for defining, training and serving neural networks. Since version 3 it runs the same code on JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch and OpenVINO, so the one thing to know before adopting it is that your backend choice, not Keras itself, determines performance.

sections.body: Keras is an open source deep learning framework written in Python and maintained by the Keras team under the Apache 2.0 licence. Its official site describes it as deep learning for humans, and the project repository shows active development continuing into late 2026. It occupies the model definition and training layer of the AI stack, sitting above numerical backends rather than replacing them. With the release of Keras 3.0, the framework became multi-backend: the same workflows can run on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch or OpenVINO for inference only. It provides the high level abstractions, layers, models, metrics, losses, optimizers and training loops, that developers use to express what a neural network should do, while the chosen backend handles tensor computation and hardware acceleration. It is not a data processing library, a serving system or a hardware runtime, and the official material does not present it as any of those.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: Keras covers the concrete jobs of deep learning work: building models, training them, evaluating them and running inference. The Sequential API suits a plain stack of layers with one input and one output tensor, while the functional API handles non-linear topology, shared layers and multiple inputs or outputs, and subclassing allows models written from scratch. Built-in methods such as fit(), evaluate() and predict() work identically across all three styles, and the site states that training and evaluation work strictly the same way across every kind of Keras model. Data can be fed as NumPy arrays, tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects or Pandas dataframes regardless of backend. The framework is strongest where a developer wants readable, concise model code that is portable across backends, and where standard architectures, convolutional, recurrent, transformer and generative, are built from well tested building blocks. The official examples span image classification, autoencoders, transfer learning, sample size estimation and text generation with a mini-GPT built through KerasHub.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Keras is designed as a high level API, and the official guides walk a beginner from a Sequential model through the functional API to custom training loops without requiring low level tensor manipulation. The site's own examples begin with loading MNIST, reshaping arrays, compiling a model with a loss, an optimizer and metrics, and calling fit(), which suggests that basic Python and a working knowledge of NumPy style arrays are the main prerequisites. Understanding what a layer, a loss function and an optimizer do helps, but the guides introduce these through working code rather than theory. Deeper work, such as writing custom layers that run across backends, requires using the keras.ops namespace, and the site notes that as long as only ops from keras.ops are used, custom layers will work with JAX, PyTorch and TensorFlow with the same code. The official material does not state formal mathematics prerequisites, and it does not present a structured curriculum for absolute beginners beyond its guides and examples.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around Keras is broad. Keras 3 implements the full Keras API across TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch, including over a hundred layers, dozens of metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, training and evaluation loops, and saving and serialization infrastructure. The keras.ops namespace provides cross-backend operations such as ops.matmul, ops.sum, ops.stack and ops.einsum, plus neural network functions such as ops.softmax, ops.binary_crossentropy and ops.conv. KerasHub supports pretrained models and components, as shown by the mini-GPT example that uses keras_hub.layers.TokenAndPositionEmbedding and TransformerDecoder layers. The site reports that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine. The repository shows more than sixty four thousand stars, and the official site offers extensive guides, examples and API documentation. The facts provided do not include details of community forums, release cadence or third party plugin registries beyond what the site states.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras is built for both quick experiments and production use, and the trade-off is largely delegated to the backend. The Sequential and functional APIs let a developer define and train a model in a few lines, and the built-in fit(), evaluate() and predict() loops remove boilerplate, which favours fast prototyping. For production, the site states that in benchmarks JAX typically delivers the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU and CPU, though results vary from model to model and non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU. A Keras model can be instantiated as a PyTorch Module, exported as a TensorFlow SavedModel or instantiated as a stateless JAX function, and saving the entire model as a single file allows recreating it later even if the code that built it is no longer available, including the optimizer state needed to resume training. The distribution API, currently implemented for the JAX backend with TensorFlow and PyTorch described as coming soon, supports model parallelism, data parallelism and combinations of both. The cost of this flexibility is that performance tuning depends on backend knowledge, and the official material does not claim that Keras itself guarantees a particular speed.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The official site states that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine, which places it among the widely used frameworks rather than a legacy choice. The repository shows active development, with a last push in October 2026, and the Keras 3 release positions it as a current standard for cross-framework model development. For someone choosing what to learn for work, that suggests Keras skills transfer across TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch environments, since existing tf.keras models that only use built-in layers can start running in JAX and PyTorch right away. The facts and the site do not provide salary data, job posting counts or a breakdown of adoption by industry, so any stronger claim about career outcomes would go beyond what is documented here.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is written in Python and is typically used alongside the backends it supports: TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch and OpenVINO for inference only. It belongs to the polyglot pattern in which a high level model definition layer stays stable while the execution engine underneath can be swapped. The site describes Keras as usable as a low-level cross-framework language to develop custom components such as layers, models or metrics that can be used in native workflows in JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch with one codebase. It also integrates with data pipelines through tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects, NumPy arrays and Pandas dataframes regardless of backend. KerasHub extends this with pretrained models and layers. The official material does not describe integrations with non-Python languages or with serving frameworks beyond the export paths it mentions, so its place beside those tools is not settled by the pages read.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: Keras is not appropriate for every model shape: the Sequential API is explicitly described as unsuitable for non-linear topology such as residual connections or multi-branch models, and those cases require the functional API or subclassing. The distribution API is currently implemented only for the JAX backend, with TensorFlow and PyTorch support described as coming soon, so large scale distributed training is not equally mature across backends. Performance depends on the backend and varies from model to model, which means Keras alone does not determine speed. The official material does not state formal prerequisites for learning, does not give a detailed comparison against other high level frameworks, and does not address serving, monitoring or deployment tooling in the pages read. Questions about long term support timelines, the maturity of the OpenVINO path and community governance are not settled by the facts or the site, and should be checked against current documentation before a decision.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
